articles.title: Muhammad Yunus' ancestral home set ablaze as violence grips Bangladesh
articles.summary: Dhaka: Crude bomb explosions rocked Bangladesh's capital before dawn, while former interim government chief Muhammad Yunus 's ancestral home was torched in Chattogram. The unrest followed a Thursday "lockdown" call by the banned Awami League, led by former prime minister Sheikh Hasina. Police and witnesses said at least four people were wounded. Witnesses reported explosions of a series of improvised devices, arson attacks and vandalism in Dhaka despite stepped-up security. Unidentified arsonists set fire to Yunus's paternal home at Chattogram's Panchlaish area after several branches of his Grameen Bank in different parts of Bangladesh were set on fire. Newspaper reports said rival activists, presumably belonging to Prime Minister Tarique Rahman's Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP), overnight attacked or set ablaze the residences of two Awami League leaders in Dhaka. Police said they stepped up security overnight, mobilising more personnel at major flyovers across the capital. At the same time, officers were seen checking vehicles at entry and exit points and questioning motorcyclists and drivers of suspicious vehicles. Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman seeks unity to halt Awami League's 'resurgence' Awami League called the lockdown coinciding with the anniversary of a special tribunal verdict sentencing Hasina to death last year after trying her in absentia on charges of committing crimes against humanity. Hasina, 79, has been living in India since fleeing Bangladesh on August 5, 2024, following a student-led protest called the July Uprising that toppled her government. Bangladesh has been seeking her extradition from India. Officials said thousands of paramilitary Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB) troops were called out to maintain order in sensitive districts including southwestern Gopalganj district, Hasina's birthplace. According to BDnews24, police arrested 565 people in a 24-hour drive in Dhaka alone ahead of the lockdown, with one prominent person being former education minister in Hasina's cabinet Nurul Islam Nahid, who was detained from his Dhaka residence at midnight on Wednesday. Prime Minister Tarique on Wednesday night sought "democratic forces" unity to prevent "resurgence" of Awami League, describing it as a "terrorist outfit" and "fallen, defeated, and ousted fascist force" and called for actions for its "decisive defeat". "Let us once again unite in the spirit of 2024, when we drove the autocratic forces out of this country, and ensure that those forces are decisively defeated," Rahman said on Tuesday night in a parliamentary address, where BNP's once ally Jamaat-e-Islami is the main opposition party. Ahead of his address at the closing sitting of the current parliamentary session, he met with party lawmakers and asked them to return immediately to their constituencies to maintain a visible presence on the streets. The Daily Star said Rahman asked BNP lawmakers not to rely solely on government machinery or the administration to counter Awami League activists, but instead to work closely with the party's grassroots leaders and workers. Police said two local ruling party leaders were killed in western Narail district when Awami League activists attacked a BNP street march. Two others, a local BNP leader and a transport worker, were killed in violence on Tuesday and Wednesday nights in southwestern Faridpur and Pirozpur. According to media reports, at least two BNP offices and one BNP leader's house were set on fire. In comparison, at least two Awami League party offices and five properties belonging to the banned party leaders were set ablaze in the past two days in different parts of Bangladesh. During the period, dozens of crude bombs were exploded, and vehicles were torched in 28 out of the country's 64 administrative districts. But clandestine attacks on Yunus's home and branches of his Grameen Bank in northeastern Sylhet, northwestern Rajshahi and southwestern Barishal and Faridpur in predawn hours or midnight in the past two days appeared as new developments. Yunus assumed power after the August 5, 2024 ouster of Hasina's Awami League government. Fresh violence grips Sheikh Hasina's hometown amid brewing tensions in Bangladesh His interim government disbanded the Awami League and sent thousands of its leaders and activists to jail, mostly on obscure or difficult-to-prove charges like mass murder and many others, including exposed lynching, when his government visibly preferred to remain silent. During the Yunus-led regime, Hasina's father and Bangladesh's founder, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's Dhanmondi residence was set on fire and levelled in several phases by his presumed supporters, who also demolished landmark installations of the 1971 Liberation War fought under Awami League leadership. The key spokesperson of his regime, Shafiqul Alam, at that time dubbed the mob as a "pressure group". The interim regime also had Hasina tried in absentia in a special tribunal, which sentenced her to death on charges of crimes against humanity through brutal actions to tame the uprising. But political tensions, however, continued to rise since July this year, when Hasina first announced her plan to return home voluntarily from India in December despite the death sentence, to face the legal procedure while the government insisted on her extradition under a bilateral treaty with New Delhi. Her renewed announcement to return home in December at "any cost" earlier this month sparked the fresh violence which initially broke out at her southwestern Tungipara sub-district hometown following arrests of dozens of youths as suspected Awami League supporters on Tuesday. A local journalist in Tungipara reported that the police had vacated the station as hundreds of people besieged it, where nearly 30 suspected activists were detained earlier. Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed pledged to identify and take stern legal action against the perpetrators of the violence, using audio and video evidence.

articles.title: Bangladesh PM Tarique Rahman seeks unity to halt Awami League's 'resurgence'
articles.summary: Dhaka: Bangladesh Prime Minister Tarique Rahman on Wednesday sought unity among "democratic forces" to prevent the "resurgence" of deposed premier Sheikh Hasina 's currently banned Awami League as political violence gripped the country over her stated plan to return home in December despite a pending death sentence. "These terrorists (Awami League activists) have once again engaged in acts of terror against the country and its people," Rahman told parliament as political violence erupted in different parts of Bangladesh, killing at least four people in the past two days. The prime minister asked all democratic political parties to unite on a single platform, as they did during the violent student-led street protest dubbed the July Uprising that toppled the Awami League government, to counter the "fallen, defeated, and ousted fascist forces" and foil their conspiracies. "Let us once again unite in the spirit of 2024, when we drove the autocratic forces out of this country, and ensure that those forces are decisively defeated," Rahman said. Despite facing 'death sentence', ousted Bangladesh PM Sheikh Hasina vows to return home next month Ahead of his valedictory speech at the current parliamentary session's closing sitting, he asked his Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) lawmakers to immediately return to their constituencies and maintain a visible presence on the streets as political violence erupted in different parts of the country. The Daily Star and other newspapers reported that Rahman asked BNP lawmakers not to rely solely on government machinery or administration to counter Awami League activists, but rather to work closely with the party's grassroots leaders and activists. The currently disbanded Awami League called a nationwide "lockdown" on Thursday, coinciding with the anniversary of a special tribunal verdict that sentenced Hasina to death last year after trying her in absentia on charges of committing crimes against humanity. The lockdown announcement prompted authorities to step up security, deploying hundreds of paramilitary troops nationwide on Wednesday. But fresh violence erupted in parts of Bangladesh on Wednesday evening when Hasina's supporters clashed with BNP activists and law enforcement personnel. At the same time, police said two local ruling party leaders were killed in western Narail district when Awami League activists attacked a BNP street march. District police chief Al Mamun Sikder said BNP's cultural wing leader Sohel Molla and farmers front leader Mohammad Shahin succumbed to their injuries while being rushed to a hospital. A transport worker was burned to death while sleeping inside a parked bus after unidentified attackers set fire to two vehicles in southwestern Pirozpur in predawn hours of Wednesday, a day after a local BNP leader, Raju Mollah, was killed during a clash between Awami League workers and police in Faridpur late Tuesday. According to media reports, at least two BNP offices and one BNP leader's house were set on fire. Additionally, at least two Awami League party offices and five properties belonging to the banned party leaders were set ablaze in different parts of Bangladesh over the past 24 hours. During the period, dozens of crude bombs were exploded, and vehicles were torched in 28 out of 64 administrative districts in the country. But attacks on former interim government chief Muhammad Yunus' Grammeen Bank branches appeared as new developments in different parts of the country, including northeastern Sylhet, northwestern Rajshahi and southwestern Barishal and Faridpur, in predawn hours or at midnight over the past two days. Yunus assumed power following the August 5, 2024, ouster of Hasina's Awami League government during a violent, student-led street protest, after his protracted dispute with the previous regime on several legal grounds. His interim government disbanded her party and sent several thousand of its leaders and activists to jail, mostly on obscure or difficult-to-prove charges like mass murder. Several others were lynched by the mob when his government visibly preferred to remain silent. During his rule, Hasina's father and Bangladesh’s founder, Sheikh Mujibur Rahman's, Dhanmondi residence was set on fire and levelled in several phases by his presumed supporters, who also demolished landmark installations of the 1971 Liberation War fought under Awami League leadership. At that time, a key spokesperson for his regime, Shafiqul Alam, dubbed the mob a "pressure group". The interim regime also had Hasina tried in absentia in a special tribunal, which sentenced her to death on charges of crimes against humanity for brutal actions taken to quell the uprising. But political tensions, however, continued to rise since July this year, when Hasina first announced her plan to return home voluntarily from India in December to face legal proceedings, despite the death sentence. The government insisted on her extradition under a bilateral treaty with New Delhi. Hasina fled to India on August 5, 2004, aboard an Air Force plane as protesters marched towards her official residence, which they also levelled that day. But the latest incidents of violence erupted afresh amid her renewed announcement to return home. Witnesses said the violence initially broke out in the Tungipara sub-district of Gopalganj following the arrest of several suspected Awami League supporters on Tuesday. A local journalist in Tungipara reported that police had vacated the station as hundreds of people besieged it, where nearly 30 suspected activists had earlier been detained. He said authorities had previously deployed platoons of the Border Guard Bangladesh (BGB), led by army officers, but they chose to remain silent as the violence persisted for hours. "During the siege, some over-enthusiastic or unruly activists set fire after freeing detained youths from the police lockup," a local leader of the banned party said on condition of anonymity. But he claimed that the police station's newly appointed officer-in-charge provoked the violence by "unnecessarily" arresting the youths to "frighten them by showing muscle, resulting in an outburst of anger from people in the neighbourhood". Home Minister Salahuddin Ahmed pledged to identify and take stern legal action against the perpetrators of the violence, using audio and video evidence. "Today or tomorrow, those who attacked the police station, assaulted or attacked law enforcement personnel, will be identified through video footage, audio recordings and photographs and be brought under the law," he said in parliament on Tuesday evening.

Bengaluru emerges as second largest AI startup cluster in Asia
articles.summary: Bengaluru has emerged as the second largest AI-native startup cluster in Asia with the city commanding 36.3% ($2.28 billion) of India’s AI startup funding, which is more than any other city. It is also home to 71% of India’s AI and deeptech unicorns created since 2023. According to the Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 released at the tech summit on Wednesday, the city has 58% share of AI startup funding in India. Approximately, $1.5 billion AI startup funding has come into Bengaluru since 2020. The total value of AI-native ecosystem is estimated at $2 billion. Of the 1,556 deep tech startups founded in Bengaluru since 2010, 1,319 are active and funded, and they have raised $3.77 billion. Of 799 native AI startups, 764 are active and funded, the report said. The funding raised by Bengaluru startups has touched $85 billion since 2010, 47% of all venture funding raised by Indian startups, with $76.5 billion of it in the past 10 years. Minister M B Patil announces plans to establish model startup parks on 1,000 acres near Bengaluru The city has 3,810 active, funded startups founded since 2010, nearly twice Mumbai’s 1,982. “Bengaluru is the birthplace of Indian technology and innovation. Every global tech wave is refactored and reverberated across the country. This is the only ecosystem on the planet that pivots effortlessly from Avarekai to AI, from vibe coding to vada-sambar, and from semiconductors to shavige,” said Siddarth Pai, founding partner and CFO of 3one4 Capital. Priyank Kharge, Minister for Home, Electronics, IT & BT and E-Governance, Government of Karnataka, released the Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 in the presence of senior officials of the Department, industry leaders, investors and startup founders. Speaking on the occasion, Kharge said, “The Bengaluru Innovation Report 2026 shows how far Karnataka’s founders have come and how much more they can build from here. Our next task is to make sure a world-class AI, quantum or semiconductor company can grow just as well in Kalaburagi, Hubballi or Mangaluru. Deep tech rewards patience, and Karnataka will stay the course.” Prepared by the Karnataka Digital Economy Mission (KDEM) together with 3one4 Capital, with data from Tracxn, the report draws on India’s own startup and market data to track Bengaluru’s talent, capital, unicorns, policy, the Beyond Bengaluru clusters and six frontier sectors. Close to 30% of India’s active, funded women-led startups in deep tech and native AI were founded in Bengaluru, and together they have raised $323.65 million. Sixteen Bengaluru-linked companies have listed since November 2024, together worth about $42 billion at listing. Bengaluru accounts for 33 of the 226 IPOs by funded companies in India in this period, and Karnataka-headquartered companies for 37, about 16% of the total. Startups in the ecosystem take about 8.2 years from founding to exit, against a global average of 11.1 years. Bengaluru’s 57 unicorns are valued at $211 billion, 44% of India’s 131 unicorns and 55.3% of their combined value, making the city the world’s fifth-largest unicorn hub and the largest outside the US, Europe and China. Bengaluru produced 46 of India’s 100 unicorns since 2020, and its startups take about six years to reach unicorn status, against seven to 11 years in other Indian hubs. The city is also home to 212 soonicorns, 36% of India’s 589 and more than Delhi NCR (134) or Mumbai (121). Its startups reach soonicorn status in about five years, faster than in any other Indian city, and about 38% of all funds raised by India’s soonicorns have gone to Bengaluru companies. The State’s ELEVATE grant-in-aid programme has backed 1,479 startups with Rs 393.58 crore since 2017, 38.6% of them beyond Bengaluru.

articles.title: Karnataka village in the shadow of the Koh-i-Noor
articles.summary: Nearly 15 years ago, Markal Kollur was a quiet village on the banks of the Krishna in Shahapur taluk of Yadgir district and few outside the region knew of it. That changed when local historians and organisations drew attention to accounts in British historical writings that linked the village to the origin of the world-famous diamond Koh-i-Noor, now displayed at the Jewel House in London. The claim that the Koh-i-Noor, one of the world’s largest cut diamonds, originated here remains contested. However, it has brought the village into discussions about the diamond’s history and prompted residents and local historians to seek recognition for its historical importance. They hope this association will eventually put Markal Kollur on the tourism map. Their claims are based on references in books by British historians and other researchers that trace the diamond’s journey from the mines of the erstwhile Golconda Sultanate to the British Empire. One such reference, according to local historians, appears in Robert Sewell’s A Forgotten Empire: Vijayanagar; A Contribution to the History of India, published in 1900. Sewell was a historian who served in the civil service of the Madras Presidency in British India. Local historians claim that the diamond was first discovered in the mines of miner Mir Jumlani at Markal Kollur, probably in 1656 and was presented to the Sultan of Golconda. Uncovering forgotten history: Deciphering the past in Talavadi’s stones Eventually, it reached the Mughal emperor Shah Jahan. They also believe that the areas surrounding Markal Kollur once had rich diamond deposits, some of which were submerged by the river over time. “Apart from Sewell’s book, we have also referred to Koh-i-Noor: The History of the World’s Most Infamous Diamond, written by William Dalrymple and Anita Anand. The authors claim that the diamond came from the mines of Kollur in Karnataka,” said advocate Arvind Mudbool, a member of the Surpur History Research Centre. He said researchers and historians would continue to press the government to develop it as a tourist destination. For the people of Markal Kollur, the possibility that the celebrated diamond may have originated in their village has become a matter of pride. The late Bhaskar Rao Mudbool, a historian and advocate who convened the Kohinoor Smaraka Hitarakshana Samithi, was among those who championed the claim. He said that the diamond, believed to have originally weighed 756 carats, was discovered in Markal Kollur. In his book, Marethuhoda Surpur Itihasa (Forgotten History of Surpur), he traces the region’s association with diamond mining. He writes that the area comprising Shahapur, Surpur, Anantapur, Karnool, Vajrakerur, Kollur and Golkonda, once under the Vijayanagara Empire, was known for its diamond deposits. He writes that the Koh-i-Noor then changed hands several times over centuries. Persian ruler Nadir Shah is said to have given it the name Koh-i-Noor, meaning ‘Mountain of Light’, in 1739. He found it when he laid siege to Delhi. It later travelled to Persia. In 1813, Persian ruler Shuja Shah gave the diamond to Maharaja Ranjit Singh of Lahore. Following the annexation of Punjab in 1849 by Sir John Lawrence, the diamond fell into British possession and was eventually presented to Queen Victoria. A river central to the village Located about 60 km from Hatti Gold Mines, India’s largest primary producer of mined gold, Markal Kollur has a population of around 6,000, most of whom depend on agriculture. Water from the Krishna river supports cultivation, while the Kollur bridge provides an important road link between Kalaburagi and Raichur districts. Built across the Krishna in 1972, downstream of the Basavasagar (Narayanapur) reservoir, the bridge has served commuters for more than five decades. But during the monsoon, the rising river frequently submerges the bridge and surrounding areas, disrupting travel and affecting agriculture. “Around 15 years ago, we never witnessed flooding. Now, the village gets submerged during water release,” said villager Valmiki Hanumanthappa, also a member of the Surpur History Research Centre. He added that the villagers are thus seeking construction of a new bridge. The district administration has prohibited sand mining along a stretch of nearly one kilometre of the riverbed near the village to protect the area believed to be associated with the Koh-i-Noor’s discovery. Development awaited According to local sources, around 25,000 tourists from neighbouring districts visit the site every year. The district administration has allotted 8 acres and 19 guntas of land adjoining the riverbank for a historical and cultural garden, with basic visitor facilities. The proposed project includes a Koh-i-Noor diamond museum, a gazebo, a viewpoint, children’s play area, a musical fountain, a theme park, a swimming pool and an open-air theatre. But the project is yet to take shape. Residents say portions of the allotted land have been encroached upon by adjoining farmers for cultivation and want the administration to prevent it. “A project of Rs 90 crore to develop the area was proposed in 2024. Once the project is approved and completed, we plan to hand over its maintenance to the gram panchayat,” said Ramachandrappa Kattimani, Assistant Director, Department of Tourism. Local activist Hanumanthappa Bhangi said sand mining in the Markal Kollur riverbed had stopped following a campaign launched by residents after historians said of the village’s connection with the Koh-i-Noor. He recalled that Shalini Rajneesh, now Chief Secretary, had taken an interest in the project when she was the regional commissioner of the Kalaburagi division. Despite this, the project has remained on the back burner. The question of its origin However, even now, not everyone is convinced that Koh-i-Noor originated in Markal Kollur. Some residents and observers argue that the available historical evidence does not conclusively establish the precise location where the diamond was discovered. “The government should conduct a proper research to establish the origin of the Koh-i-Noor diamond,” said villager Veeresh Chalavadi. Another widely cited account traces the diamond to the Kollur mines along the Krishna in present-day Guntur district of Andhra Pradesh, during the reign of the Kakatiya dynasty. From there, it is believed to have passed through several royal hands across Asia and Europe before reaching the British. The competing accounts have left the precise origins of the Koh-i-Noor open to debate. But the association has already brought visibility to Markal Kollur that was once little known beyond its immediate surroundings. Whether or not the historical claim is eventually established, residents hope that the attention will lead to better connectivity, tourism infrastructure and livelihood opportunities.

articles.title: Symbols that celebrate Karnataka
articles.summary: Karnataka recently became the first state in India to officially designate a state amphibian: the Malabar tree toad, scientifically known as Pedostibes tuberculosus (PeTu) and locally called Malenadina Mara Gantikappe. The tiny toad was chosen for its close association with the Western Ghats and its importance as an indicator of the health of evergreen forest. Its recognition has added another dimension to Karnataka’s list of natural and cultural symbols. The Asian elephant is the state’s animal, the Indian roller (Neelakantha) its bird, the lotus its flower, sandalwood its tree, mango its fruit, the Sahyadri birdwing its butterfly and the carnatic carp its fish. As per experts, state symbols are often regarded as emblems of regional pride, and their significance goes beyond identity. They can draw public attention to native species, ecosystems and conservation challenges while creating a sense of collective responsibility towards protecting biodiversity and preserving cultural traditions. There is no uniform, prescribed procedure for selecting a species or art form as a state symbol. Governments generally consult experts before making such declarations. Ecological significance, geographical distribution, cultural association and the need to highlight lesser-known biodiversity are among the considerations. PeTu’s leap towards conservation For batrachologist Gururaja K V, whose efforts led to the Malabar tree toad being identified as Karnataka’s state amphibian, PeTu is a particularly interesting addition to the state symbols. “Unlike many familiar toads that spend much of their time on the ground, PeTu is largely arboreal, living among trees and vegetation in the Western Ghats,” he says. Uncovering forgotten history: Deciphering the past in Talavadi’s stones He says its recognition also brings attention to a group of animals that often remain outside mainstream conservation discussions. Amphibians are particularly sensitive to environmental changes, including habitat degradation, pollution and alterations in rainfall patterns. “While the Malabar tree toad is an ecological indicator species, the idea behind designating it as the state amphibian was to raise awareness about its importance and educate people about amphibians. Through this recognition, we hope to spark children's curiosity about frogs and the ecosystems they inhabit,” Gururaja adds. Wings of the Western Ghats The Sahyadri Birdwing, also known as the Southern Birdwing, has been designated Karnataka’s state butterfly. Krushnamegh Kunte, associate professor at the National Centre for Biological Sciences (NCBS), Bengaluru, and a butterfly biologist, says the endemic species is among India’s largest butterflies, with predominantly black wings. He says its selection reflects Karnataka’s biological richness and the diversity of the Western Ghats, while its red and yellow colours resemble those of the state flag, linking it to Karnataka’s cultural identity. He adds that the recognition of the Sahyadri Birdwing as the state butterfly could help people, particularly younger generations, connect with the natural heritage of the Western Ghats and raise awareness about the need to protect lesser-known species and their habitats. The spectacular Neelakantha While the Malabar tree toad and Sahyadri birdwing may be unfamiliar to many, Karnataka’s state bird, the Indian roller, is a far more recognisable presence. Its brilliant shades of blue and turquoise shine in sunlight, while its spectacular mid-air acrobatics, particularly during courtship and territorial displays, make it a captivating sight across the state’s open landscapes. Senior birder S Subramanya says the Indian roller, also known as Neelakantha, is deeply rooted in Karnataka’s natural heritage. “The bird is an important part of our rural landscapes, particularly open grasslands, agricultural fields and open scrub habitats,” he says. He adds that the bird plays an important ecological role by feeding on insects and other small creatures, helping maintain ecological balance. Its selection as the state bird also gives recognition to a species familiar to people across Karnataka. However, familiarity does not necessarily guarantee its protection. “A recent scientific study shows that over the years, its population has decreased considerably and this can largely be attributed to loss of suitable habitat, consequent decline in food availability and nest-site limitations, which may be probably tied to land-use changes in recent decades,” says Subramanya, stressing on stepping up conservation measures. The fragrant sandalwood Sandalwood has earned Karnataka the popular identity of ‘Gandhada Gudi’ and is recognised well beyond the country’s borders. From religious rituals and traditional medicine to carving, perfumery and handicrafts, sandalwood has occupied an important place in Karnataka’s cultural and economic landscape. Mysuru, in particular, became synonymous with sandalwood products. The state’s association with the fragrant tree dates back centuries, with successive kingdoms patronising its cultivation and trade. Documents and travel accounts of foreign visitors record that the Vijayanagara Empire used sandalwood as a valuable resource in its trade networks during the 14th and 16th centuries. Tipu Sultan declared it a ‘Royal tree’ in 1792, while the Mysuru Wadiyars promoted sandalwood as a premium product, taking its fragrance to international markets. A N Arun Kumar, scientist at the Institute of Wood Science and Technology, Bengaluru, and an expert in sandalwood research, says, “Sandalwood is an apt choice as Karnataka’s state tree because of its biological, economic and cultural significance. The species is closely associated with the state’s forests and has shaped its cultural and religious traditions, handicrafts and economic history.” He adds that successive governments have revised sandalwood policies since 2001–02 to revive sandalwood cultivation across the state. In the early 1980s, India’s first sandalwood survey recorded Karnataka as having nearly 58% of the country’s sandalwood-bearing area. With the state government relaxing policies, more farmers are now growing the tree across Karnataka. According to recent reports, around 700 farmers are cultivating sandalwood on more than 4,000 acres in the state. A symbol of strength and stewardship The elephant, Karnataka’s state animal, is another symbol that brings together ecology and culture. Karnataka is home to one of the largest elephant populations in the country. The animal is deeply embedded in the state’s history, from Hoysala and Vijayanagara sculptures to the Mysuru Dasara celebrations. Raman Sukumar, former chairperson of the Elephant Task Force, says, “Karnataka has a long association with elephants, both in its forests and cultural traditions, particularly the Mysuru Dasara celebrations. As an ecological keystone species, elephants play a crucial role in maintaining forest ecosystems. Their selection as the state animal recognises this close relationship between nature and society,” he says. A fruit woven into Karnataka’s identity Mango, Karnataka’s state fruit, is as much a part of its cultural identity as it is of its agricultural economy. Its diversity of varieties, flavours and traditional uses makes it a familiar presence across the state. S V Hittalmani, former additional director (fruits) of Horticulture, says the diversity of mangoes produced in the state makes it a fitting choice as Karnataka’s state fruit. “Mango represents not just the state’s agricultural wealth but also its culture, traditions and food habits. It is one fruit that connects almost every region of Karnataka, with each belt having its own varieties, flavours and culinary preferences. Karnataka has a rich diversity of mangoes, including Alphonso or Aapus, Badami, Raspuri, Totapuri, Neelam, Banganapalli, Mallika, Malgova, Kesar and several local varieties such as Kari Ishad, Mundappa and Nekkare,” he says. Karnataka cultivates mangoes on nearly 1.6 lakh to 1.7 lakh hectares, making it one of the state’s major horticultural crops. “Beyond its economic importance, mango has a deep cultural connection. Tender mango leaves are used to decorate entrances during festivals and auspicious occasions, while raw mangoes are an essential ingredient in pickles and traditional preparations. Mango is also an integral part of Ugadi celebrations, with its seasonal arrival coinciding with the beginning of the Hindu New Year,” he says. “The fruit may be available for only three to four months of the year, but the craze and enthusiasm it generates among people last throughout the year,” he says. Mango also has considerable economic value through exports and its use in food-processing industries. However, its susceptibility to changing weather conditions has affected cultivation over the years, posing challenges to growers.

The average wind speed along the Odisha coast would be around 100 kmph, he said. The Odisha government has also announced the closure of schools in six districts for three days from Thursday – Ganjam, Gajapati, Puri, Jagatsinghpur, Kendrapara and Kandhamal – suspended leaves of employees, and deployed senior bureaucrats in vulnerable areas in the wake of the approaching cyclone.
